item.title: 2. Larger Pacific Striped Octopus
item.description:
39 points by olalonde on 2026-09-09T04:32:22

The Larger Pacific Striped Octopus (LPSO), also known as the Harlequin octopus, is a species first documented in the 1970s that remains scientifically undescribed and lacks an official scientific name. Found in tropical waters of the Eastern Pacific—from Panama and Guatemala to Mexico and Colombia—it prefers soft muddy or sandy substrates at depths of 7–100 meters. Unlike most solitary octopus species, LPSO is gregarious, forming colonies of up to 40 individuals whose dens sit within one meter of each other. It displays three body color patterns—completely pale, completely dark brown, and a unique "stripe-bar-spot" pattern—and exhibits distinctive behaviors including intimate beak-to-beak mating without cannibalism, pair bonding through food and den sharing, and iteroparity (spawning multiple times across its roughly two-year lifespan). Females brood eggs in pairs within their dens, tending them until hatching, after which offspring are pelagic until adulthood. LPSO hunts shrimp, crabs, stomatopods, and bivalves using stalking, chasing, and ambush methods, drilling holes into larger prey. The species undergoes senescence before death, with males typically surviving 1–2 weeks and females 2–4 months after the onset of this stage.

  2. Something about seeing "gregarious nature" used to describe a non-human animal feels so... whimsical? I like it. Likewise with "intimate embrace" and other descriptions that follow.
  3. One critical feature of these octopuses is that they don't just die after mating (most species of octopus do)... Which opens up possibilities, like teaching their young skills they have acquired.

item.title: 4. Growing proof that autonomous cars save lives
item.description:
326 points by bookofjoe on 2026-09-09T17:14:59

Mounting research indicates that self-driving vehicles and advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS) significantly reduce crashes and injuries compared to human drivers. Studies show automatic emergency braking (AEB) can cut pedestrian crashes by 27% and rear-end crashes by 50%, while bundled ADAS features reduce insurance claims by up to 39%. Waymo's robotaxis, with over 20 million paid rides, demonstrated 92% fewer fatal or serious-injury crashes in an independent study, a finding broadly supported by separate Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) research showing 68% fewer overall crashes across several cities. Experts and medical professionals argue that this technology represents a critical public-health intervention, with the potential to prevent tens of thousands of annual U.S. deaths and over a million globally. While the industry still lacks uniform national standards, recent developments include federal exemptions for new vehicle designs and partnerships to establish performance criteria.

Comment Link

Top Comments

  1. Better driver education and higher test standards would save lives too. So would banning alcohol. None of these solutions, including automated cars, will be mandated any time soon. It's not enough to have data, you also have to have societal buy-in.Interesting that Waymo chooses to compare accident rates with the average driver vs the rideshare drivers their cars replace. The numbers wouldn't look as impressive because rideshare drivers are involved in fewer serious accidents than the average person.Waymo says it has 170 million miles and I found 2 fatal accidents it was involved in (fault doesn't matter as fault is not included in the other stat either). Looks like the average is about 1.3 fatalities per 100 million miles, and about 1 per 100 million miles for CDLs. This doesn't seem that impressive.If we want adoption, we would need it be placed in individual vehicles and it should look at removing driver liability. People will use it when they are drunk if it means not going to jail and it's readily available.
  2. Fatality data is extremely skewed. 44% of drivers aren't using a seatbelt, 29% are speeding related, I recall alcohol involvement being about 30%, though it's not listed in the link I checked. About 20% of automobile fatalities aren't in cars but are pedestrians or bicyclists struck by cars (add another 16% if you want to include motorcyclists, though only half of which involve another vehicle). I recall the percentage of vulnerable road user deaths is much higher in urban areas.(https://www.iihs.org/research-areas/fatality-statistics/deta...)The majority of drivers are good, but some drivers are really bad. Life in USA is extremely car-centric and taking away a license is often infeasible and the offender usually drives without their license anyways. If anything, I'd like autonomous cars to give a legal out to remove bad drivers. You get a DUI, or commonly speeding? You may only take an autocar.
  3. I'd much rather all of the resources that are going into autonomous cars was instead going into proper public transit infrastructure. Cars are so hopelessly space and energy inefficient, and I hate driving them. If I could get around by bus, light rail, bike, and all of the wasted city space devoted to parking could be turned into more housing and amenities, that would be great.I think it would be meaningful to also compare the fatality rates of the time tested and proven forms of public transit to these self driving cars too.

item.title: 7. GPT-6 Astra, looped transformers, and hidden reasoning
item.description:
404 points by ModelForge on 2026-09-09T14:37:47

OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra has been released with significant improvements over its predecessor GPT-5.6, particularly excelling in 3D rendering, animation, and computer-use tasks where the model interacts with graphical user interfaces on local machines. It achieves 99.9% on the ARC-AGI-3 benchmark and performs strongly in math, coding, and agentic coding tasks, though independent benchmark comparisons show it doesn't always pull ahead by large margins across all harnesses. The model is trained using reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) and computer-use training, where Apple Macs serve as environments exposing macOS interfaces for the model to learn mouse and keyboard interactions through repeated cycles of screenshotting, action prediction, and execution feedback. Rumors suggest Astra may use a "looped transformer" or "recurrent depth" architecture, which is not a new concept but involves passing intermediate representations through the same stack of transformer blocks multiple times, reusing weights rather than adding distinct blocks—similar to the 2018 Universal Transformer approach. This architecture may relate to speculation that Astra hides its reasoning traces (chains of thought), though the article aims to clarify the relationship between looped transformers and chain-of-thought transparency. Additionally, the author suggests that users may want to update or simplify existing instruction files like AGENTS.md and SKILL.md, as newer LLMs have become more efficient at understanding prompts without extensive hand-holding.

Comment Link

Top Comments

  1. For the research focused, there are some references in my blogpost here on what kinds of computational problems minimally require how much CoT to solve: https://blog.wtf.sg/posts/2023-02-03-the-new-xor-problem/Notably Will Merrill's work: https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.07923As for how universal transformers (looping transformers, but everyone has since forgotten prior work) will affect this, Will Merrill (again) has a paper here (https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.03961) that discusses exactly this.The original universal transformers is called "universal" because if you allow for per-token looping decisions, it can theoretically be Turing complete without needing CoT (some nuance here about levels of precision used).As for whether having little or no CoT is "unsafe": It isn't clear that the model's CoT reveal how they actually arrive at the answer. As an example, what if they provide an answer before the CoT? (https://arxiv.org/html/2603.01437v2) If this is already in question, we shouldn't be relying on the CoT for monitoring the model's reasoning.As always there is a lot of nuance to the topic once you get your hands dirty with the details.
  2. I gave owao/Nanbeige4.2-3B-GGUF (Q8 quant) a try to understand how loop transformers work and compare it with other models especially with Ling 3 Tiny MoE model. As reported in the article, it is compute intensive (due to looped layers) and made a mistake during tool call just like how Ling 3 Tiny MoE did for exactly the same prompt.
  3. If you loop an entire transformer model on itself, that seems like by-definition hidden reasoning.If the output of the model is its reasoning trace, and you simply feed that back into the model again at inference time instead of outputting it - then it is by definition hidden (but I would expect you could pull both this trace and a further-down final output trace out)

item.title: 9. Show HN: Compute polynomials twice as fast
item.description:
75 points by thomasahle on 2026-09-09T08:53:58

For evaluating polynomials, a preprocessing technique on coefficients can reduce the number of multiplications to ⌊n/2⌋+1 for a monic polynomial (n−1 multiplications via Horner's method), with one additional multiplication for a general polynomial. This method is applicable to approximating functions (like exp, sin, cos) and to uses in cryptography, hashing, and coding theory. The associated tool allows users to input any polynomial and select a field, after which it performs the preprocessing.

Comment Link

I only knew Horner and Estrin, but I think I've gotten a grasp on most of them.One small change I'd recommend is for the graph visualization, have a separate source node for each x, x^2, x^4 used. A single x source clutters the graph and hides the structure.

item.title: 10. Automattic's board forces CEO Matt Mullenweg into leave of absence
item.description:
227 points by LeoPanthera on 2026-09-09T23:49:29

Matt Mullenweg, founder and CEO of Automattic (parent company of WordPress.com, Tumblr, WooCommerce, and Pocket Casts), was placed on paid leave of absence by his company's board against his will. According to a Slack message Mullenweg sent to employees, CFO Mark Davies conspired with board members Ann Dunwoody, Toni Schneider, and Sue Decker to vote for the leave, with Davies installed as interim CEO. Mullenweg said he voted against the action and was denied time to have it reviewed by legal counsel, receiving the resolution just 50 minutes before the meeting. WordPress.org executive director Mary Hubbard confirmed the status change but said the open-source WordPress project remains unaffected. Automattic confirmed the leave in a statement expressing confidence in Davies' leadership. The move comes amid ongoing controversy, including a protracted lawsuit with WordPress hosting competitor WP Engine over royalty fees and allegations of abuse of power, a 2024 episode in which Mullenweg told employees who disagreed with him to quit (159 did), threats to deactivate community members' accounts over a forked WordPress project, and a 16% staff layoff in April 2025. The exact reason for the board's decision remains unclear, though some speculated it may relate to Mullenweg's recent return from the Burning Man festival.

item.title: 11. Factoring RSA 260
item.description:
84 points by samyok on 2026-09-09T20:16:08

Eric Lu used the Devin AI to optimize the CADO-NFS general number field sieve (GNFS) for GPU, developing a drop-in replacement for the CPU lattice siever and accelerating the entire factoring pipeline. Across a three-week project with multiple concurrent AI sessions, they iteratively optimized polynomial selection, lattice sieving, and linear algebra, scaling from 155-digit to 260-digit factorizations. The GPU-accelerated pipeline successfully factored RSA-260 (a 260-digit number) in approximately 15.5 days (1,344,878 seconds), demonstrating significant performance improvements over traditional CPU-based methods and showcasing the ability of AI agents to handle complex computational number theory tasks at scale, while relying on human guidance for executive direction and optimization strategy.

item.title: 12. Qwen 3.8 follows GPT-5.5 Pro reasoning prefills
item.description:
207 points by wsxiaoys on 2026-09-09T17:24:28

This experiment tests how inserting the initial 1% of reasoning from the teacher model GPT-5.5 Pro into various open models affects their final answer generation, measuring the recall of the teacher's answer in the first 100 tokens. Across 45 problems, the Qwen3.8 A95B model showed the largest positive effect, with its recall score increasing by 18.18 percentage points to 34.97%, strongly suggesting its training data may have included outputs from GPT-5.5 Pro or a closely related model. In contrast, Kimi K3 had the highest baseline overlap with GPT-5.5 Pro (31.11% unprefilled) but gained only 4.54 points from the prefill. The benefit was most pronounced for STEM problems, where recall jumped by 26.99 points when using the prefill.

Comment Link

Top Comments

  1. That writing style might be a tad too tenseIf I got it correct (appending B from https://stolen-thoughts.com/paper.pdf is essential) they are the authors of the well-known exploit to recover readable CoT from OpenAI and Anthropic models. They use that to find hints of distillation, by running a benchmark with a SotA model, recovering the CoT, then taking the first 1% of the CoT and running the open-source model as if that was the start of its own CoT. In the paper they found that Kimi-K3 gets a lot closer to Claude 4.8 answers when prefilled with the start of Claude 4.8 reasoning, suggesting that Claude 4.8 was used in its post-training. This blog post is the follow-up with results that suggest that Qwen3.8 was post-trained with the help of GPT-5.5 Pro (or some similarly responding GPT model, it's unclear how many models they tested)
  2. I wasn't aware that we have access to raw reasoning tokens? I thought what you get is a kind of summary. Does the author have some kind of privileged access or was my assumption wrong?But for the question studied here it probably doesn't matter - overlaps in the publicly available output may be indicative of distillation (or not), regardless of what it is. I would just find it surprising that the Chinese labs would use it so trustingly. The publicly released reasoning trace is the first place where I would suspect some distillation poisoning to be injected.
  3. I see comments that this overlap between Qwen and GPT is due to rogue training or post hoc training. Did it occur to anyone that maybe the two sets of models were trained directly on the same solutions to the researchers' benchmark?

item.title: 13. Desert Ant Labs: local, fast models that run on device
item.description:
435 points by willwhitedc on 2026-09-09T11:39:46

Desert Ant Labs is a European AI lab specializing in on-device intelligence, offering a suite of small, fast, and specialized models for audio, vision, and text that run directly on devices like smartphones without incurring cloud costs. Their initial launch includes 18 models—12 stable and 6 in beta—accessible via a single SDK for Swift, Kotlin, and JavaScript, designed to be dropped into apps with minimal code. Key models include Voz (transcription 4.7x faster than Whisper), Clear (audio enhancement), Redact (real-time PII masking in 27 languages), and Tongue (lightweight language identification), all optimized for speed and low resource usage. The models are free for up to 100,000 monthly active devices, requiring no tokens or logins, and emphasize data privacy by keeping processing local. Developed from the team’s experience building the video app Detail, Desert Ant Labs aims to replace cloud-dependent AI with efficient, task-specific on-device models, arguing that the world's existing device compute power makes this a sovereign and cost-effective alternative to data center-centric AI.

Comment Link

Top Comments

  1. This is a cool way of approaching AI models. I'm a big fan of local LLMs, local specific models like this should be even more powerful.> Every model is free up to 100k monthly active devices. No tokens, no logins.I dunno about the business model though. Cloud LLM billing makes sense: you're getting another computer to do work with each request, and using their compute via their gateway that they bill you.These local models are like old school software. They're producing the weights, and then giving them to people. If I'm happy with the weights you've given me, and I'm not using your compute for inference and not wanting or needing any updates off you, why should you continue getting money off me and my customers?The whole "but we need to keep it updated for your security" doesn't really work as well for software designed to run fully offline like these local models are.I'm not saying they shouldn't get paid, but I guess I feel a personal sadness that it's less obvious how to successfully monetise such a sincerely useful and beneficial approach towards AI models.

I’ve been looking for something tiny I could embed in a webapp. Not a full genius model, just something light which could enhance the product without requiring ongoing cost.Most organisations give their users terrible hardware, so anything which requires 32GB of RAM or a MacBook Pro won’t work if it’s a government or large organisation.
  3. > The world ships more than a billion capable phones, tablets, and laptops a year, most with a chip built for exactly this work, paid for and idle most of the day. Run the model there and the economics flip: no per-call cost, no round-trip, and nothing leaves the device.This. I run small models (>50MB) for bio-imaging/biotech applications, it feels like every README implies that you need a discrete GPU to get started. While some do, many, especially the most useful ones, do not. Sure it matters if you're also going to do fine-tuning, but I believe your typical user just wants to detect some nuclei and get some cell-body ratios.The laptop on your desk won't be running Meta's SAM, but it has more than enough compute to crunch 100's of your H&E slides overnight.

item.title: 19. Understanding the recent DDoS attack against Read the Docs
item.description:
187 points by davidfischer on 2026-09-09T15:55:53

In mid-to-late June 2026, Read the Docs suffered its largest-ever DDoS attack, peaking at 5.5 million requests per minute—100 times its normal traffic—and lasting nearly ten days. The attack was highly sophisticated, featuring massive volume from millions of global IPs, randomized headers and TLS parameters to evade detection, and deliberate targeting of uncached URLs like 404 errors and redirects to bypass defenses. Traditional IP blocking was ineffective, and attackers used adaptive, "yo-yo" patterns to probe rate limits and maximize infrastructure costs. The company defended itself by aggressively caching all content (even errors and redirects), deploying targeted rate limiting and bot detection focused on request characteristics rather than IPs, and using Infrastructure as Code for rapid rule deployment. Key lessons learned include the obsolescence of IP blocking for distributed attacks, the critical importance of caching non-cacheable paths, and the need for layered, intelligent defenses that balance protection with minimal friction for legitimate users.

Low reputation IPs get stalled for longer and the requests that exceed the queue get dropped. The idea is graceful degradation:A good rep IP will not be stalled by sleep(). A bad rep IP will be slowed down by the wait times + rate-limits (queue exceeded) before getting completely banned for good. The point is to have more granularity before throwing errors at random users at the server-level.

item.title: 21. Lotus Notes and the dangers of starting from scratch
item.description:

Lotus Notes, launched in 1989, was a pioneering collaboration and database platform that predated many standard email features like encryption, rich text formatting, and attachments, stemming from an earlier 1970s system called PLATO Notes. Conceived by Ray Ozzie as a way to recreate PLATO's community-driven environment, it allowed organizations to build custom applications, share synchronized databases, and communicate through forums or email-like notes, far beyond traditional email. While lauded for its powerful, cross-platform capabilities and integration of features like notifications and threaded messages, its non-standard, often counterintuitive user interface—marked by unique shortcuts and design choices—frustrated many users, contributing to a divided reception. Despite its advanced groupware potential, it struggled with usability and adaptation, leading to competition from Microsoft and others, yet its core design influenced modern collaboration tools, and it persisted in various forms.

item.title: 23. Why Emacs Consult async searches feel slow and how to speed them up
item.description:
54 points by mpweiher on 2026-09-09T17:13:43

Consult is an Emacs package for asynchronous file and search commands that intentionally uses conservative default delays to manage background processes. The behavior is controlled by three key variables: `consult-async-input-debounce` (which delays starting a search until typing pauses), `consult-async-input-throttle` (which sets a hard rate limit on process starts), and `consult-async-refresh-delay` (which controls how often the UI updates with new results). These can be set to lower values (e.g., 0.05 seconds) for a more responsive feel, but this trades increased CPU and battery usage for reduced input latency, making it more suitable for plugged-in desktops than for laptops or very large projects.

item.title: 30. Playing whack-a-mole is losing
item.description:
60 points by surprisetalk on 2026-09-09T13:41:53

In security engineering, two distinct philosophies emerge among professionals: "Security as Identity," which frames security work as a counterculture identity built around cleverly discovering and exploiting unexpected vulnerabilities, often prioritizing the thrill of finding bugs, and "Security as Robustness," which views security as an integral part of building correct, reliable systems that maintain their properties under all conditions, including attacks. While the hacker mindset is valuable for understanding failure modes, a primary focus on identity can lead to a "whack-a-mole" approach—continuously finding and patching issues without addressing root causes, which is ultimately a losing strategy. In contrast, the robustness approach treats security incidents as diagnostic failures and aims for systemic prevention, using tools like vulnerability reward programs (VRPs) not just to enumerate bugs, but to inform a strategy that reduces the incidence of entire bug classes over time. True security success is measured not by how many issues are resolved, but by whether the system is becoming inherently more secure and resilient.

item.title: 34. Show HN: Geiger – See every AI agent on your machine and what it can touch
item.description:
45 points by atomburst on 2026-09-09T14:54:49

Geiger is a read-only, no-install command-line tool (npx geiger-scan) that inventories every AI agent, model-context-protocol (MCP) server, plugin, and AI extension on a machine, reporting in plain language what each component can execute, access, or hold (like credentials). It scans standard configuration directories for ecosystems like Claude Code, MCP hosts, other AI CLIs, editor extensions, and browser extensions, outputting findings with origin, capability tags (e.g., EXECUTES, HOLDS-SECRETS, BROAD-FILESYSTEM), and evidence paths, without writing data or phoning home unless the user explicitly requests a JSON file. Designed for both individual and fleet (MSP/IT) use, it supports HTML reports, machine-readable JSON output for drift detection (via --diff and --strict modes), and prioritizes transparency and security by revealing policy wrappers and never exposing secret values. While it provides an initial inventory rather than a full security audit—only seeing known config paths and not runtime behavior—its open-source, dependency-free codebase is published with provenance, and it is maintained as a free tool by Atomburst.

item.title: 37. The Invention of the MMO
item.description:
38 points by devitoria on 2026-09-09T16:38:14

The Commodore 64, introduced in 1982, was a best-selling home computer noted for its low price and advanced sound and graphics capabilities, which made it a popular gaming platform. It later enabled access to the QuantumLink (Q-Link) online network, which hosted Habitat—a pioneering virtual world developed by Lucasfilm Games in the mid-1980s. Habitat pioneered concepts like avatars, in-game currency, player-driven economies, and persistent online communities where users could socialize, trade, customize characters, and engage in unscripted activities. The game’s open-ended design led to unpredictable social dynamics, from economic exploits and bugs to the emergence of user-created performing arts, illustrating early lessons about online interaction, community, and governance in digital worlds. Despite technical limitations and high connection costs, Habitat demonstrated the potential for large-scale, persistent virtual societies and established foundational principles for future online games and social platforms.

item.title: 39. On Really Trying (2009)
item.description:
103 points by whoami_nr on 2026-09-09T06:58:44

Knowing that a problem is solvable and that progress is possible creates powerful motivation and accelerates breakthroughs, as illustrated by various historical and anecdotal examples. People like students tasked with finding quantum gravity, statisticians solving famous problems thought to be homework, and researchers chasing computational breakthroughs perform best when assured an answer exists and urgency is applied. Conviction that a solution is achievable, combined with direct evidence from others' success or clear hints, often overcomes psychological barriers and bureaucratic slowness that normally impede scientific progress. Ultimately, the key factor is not innate genius but the psychological shift that occurs when one accepts the task must and can be accomplished now.

item.title: 41. The State of Allocators in 2026 – 6 Months Later
item.description:
15 points by aw1621107 on 2026-09-09T16:23:47

Significant progress has been made in stabilizing custom allocators in Rust, driven primarily by Nia and the libs team. The core `Allocator` trait is being finalized with a minimal interface containing `allocate` and `deallocate` methods, and it will be made dyn-compatible from the start, enabling dynamic dispatch similar to Zig's default approach. This initial stabilization is an MVP, starting with support for `Vec` and `Box` but excluding methods for other container types like `BTreeMap` until further work is done. Key design decisions include prohibiting unwinding from allocator methods to prevent unsound states, and addressing complex interactions with other Rust features. The safe `Clone` trait is not suitable for cloning allocators due to potential double-free issues; a new unsafe marker trait (`AllocatorClone`) is proposed to provide stronger guarantees. Additionally, integrating allocators with `Pin` requires careful handling to ensure pinned values are properly dropped before their memory is invalidated, preventing unsoundness when memory is reset or reused. This first stabilization provides the essential foundation for custom allocators, with ongoing work focused on expanding functionality and ensuring soundness across more advanced use cases.

item.title: 46. Is OpenAI Taking Everyone for Fools?
item.description:
71 points by lcubw on 2026-09-09T17:09:51

On September 8, 2026, mathematicians Tristan Buckmaster and Levent Alpöge publicly announced a solution to a decades-old problem concerning the Navier-Stokes equations. Simultaneously, OpenAI published its own claim to have independently solved the same problem. Buckmaster alleges that OpenAI began its effort only after hearing a rumor about the researchers' progress and that the company later tried to exclude Alpöge from authorship, citing his employment with a rival firm. OpenAI's press release acknowledges starting work after the rumor but states it is "unlikely" but cannot rule out that de-identified data from researchers' private use of its Codex product may have been used to train its model. This incident raises serious concerns about potential scientific misconduct and data privacy, as OpenAI cannot verify the training data source. The controversy casts doubt on the credibility of the company's claimed breakthroughs and serves as a warning to researchers about the risks of using its tools.

item.title: 3. How to build a printer
item.description:
300 points by cat-whisperer on 2026-09-08T21:22:11

A developer modified an Xteink X3 e-ink reader to function as a wireless printer by implementing Internet Printing Protocol (IPP) on the device itself. After finding the original upload workflow tedious, they built a printer server that announces itself via Bonjour as "penguin," accepts monochrome raster print jobs from macOS in driverless mode, and renders pages directly to the e-ink display. The key technical breakthrough was bypassing the device's severe RAM limitations (400 KB total, with only 6.8 KB free after Wi-Fi startup) by streaming decoded, scaled, and dithered pixel data straight to the display's reserved screen memory row by row, eliminating the need to buffer a full 8.4 MB page image. This reduced image-buffer RAM usage from roughly 113 KB to 62 KB, freeing space for network socket buffers. The result is a device that appears as "penguin" in the macOS print dialog, renders pages in about a second, and stores saved printouts as BMP files on the SD card for later browsing—a folder serving as the output tray. The full implementation, including the printer server, is available in the developer's CrossPoint firmware fork.

Comment Link

Top Comments

  1. >penguin would shrink the result to fit its screen. >I declared A5 and Letter paper, media type stationery, and an output bin called face-up.You can (and should!) define exact dimensions of your screen in `media-size-supported`. It will probably be a non-standard IPP name, that's why you should define that in `media-supported` as `om_NNNmmxYYYmm` or `oe_NNNinxYYYin`That way you don't need to scale the incoming data, the PC will format it exactly to the dimensions of the screen.Both PWG Raster and Apple Raster support 1-bit-per-pixel mode (instead of 8-bit-per-pixel you use), that's why the input could be 8 times less in size. Use `print-color-mode-{supported,default}=bi-level` instead of `monochrome` for that. And also tune `urf-supported`'s `W` option, use `W1` for this case.The screen/dithering could be ass in 1-bit mode, see https://github.com/OpenPrinting/libcupsfilters/pull/160 where I added more dithering options (Linux-only though, Apple seems to abandon their CUPS).

item.title: 8. I-have-ADHD: A skill to stop coding agents from burying the answer
item.description:
418 points by domhudson on 2026-09-08T14:13:26

The i-have-adhd skill is a plugin for coding assistants (such as Claude Code) that restructures AI responses to be ADHD-friendly by prioritizing action over preamble. It enforces 10 rules: lead with the next action, number multi-step tasks, end with one concrete next step, suppress tangents, restate state each turn, include specific time estimates, make wins visible, provide matter-of-fact error messages, cap lists at 5 items, and avoid preamble, recaps, or closers like "Hope this helps!" A typical response is rewritten from verbose, exploratory paragraphs into concise, numbered steps with a clear next action. The plugin is loosely based on *The Adult ADHD Tool Kit* by J. Russell Ramsay and Anthony L. Rostain, adapted for how an LLM should respond rather than how a human should organize their day. It is MIT-licensed, available in multiple languages (English, Chinese, Portuguese, Japanese, Vietnamese, Korean, Thai), and installable via a GitHub repository with optional forking to customize the SKILL.md file.

item.title: 11. Benchmarking Qwen3.8 27B quantizations: 4-bit holds up, 1-bit collapses
item.description:
245 points by stared on 2026-09-08T14:49:19

The Qwen3.8 27B model in its full BF16 format requires 55GB of GPU memory, exceeding most consumer hardware. However, a 4-bit quantized version (Q4_K_M) at 17GB fits on a 24GB card like the RTX 4090 and performs identically to the full model on the agentic coding benchmark Terminal-Bench 2.1. Testing across GPQA Diamond and IFBench shows negligible performance loss down to 4-bit quantization. A 2-bit quantization (10.7GB) causes a slight drop in some tasks but remains functional, while 1-bit quantizations collapse to random-chance performance. Benchmarking costs on rented GPUs ranged from about $167 for a 1-bit model to over $2,300 for the full BF16 model on Terminal-Bench 2.1. For most users, the 4-bit quantization offers a practical balance, fitting within typical VRAM limits while maintaining quality for most tasks.

item.title: 13. A Topological Picture Book, Rendered
item.description:
93 points by mathgenius on 2026-09-08T22:28:14

This page presents an interactive 3D renderer that visualizes mathematical surfaces using a hand-drawn ink illustration style inspired by mid-century artists like Francis and Apéry. The rendering is created with tapered ribbon strokes rather than pixels, employing techniques such as silhouette contours, principal-curvature hatching, cross-hatching for darker tones, and visibility handling with dashed hidden lines and paper haloes. The system can display surfaces like Boy's surface and Morin's surface, with an interface allowing users to rotate and zoom the model. Users can input custom surface formulas using JavaScript expressions and built-in functions. The artistic effects include ink pooling at stroke starts, ragged bleed into simulated paper grain, and hand-lettered labels that dim when their associated point is hidden, all aiming for a sketchy, illustrative aesthetic rather than photorealism.

item.title: 15. Animation in Bevy: The Big Picture
item.description:
65 points by ibobev on 2026-09-08T20:08:44

To play a 3D character animation from a .glb file in a Bevy application, you need an `AnimationPlayer` component and an `AnimationGraph`. The `AnimationPlayer` is automatically inserted into an entity within the model's hierarchy when it is spawned. An `AnimationGraph` stores the animation data, and a `NodeIndex` specifies which animation within the graph to use. To connect them, you must locate the entity containing the `AnimationPlayer` (often by iterating through the scene hierarchy), add an `AnimationGraphHandle` component to it, and then call `player.play(index)`. The official example demonstrates this by loading the animation clip and scene from a .glb file, spawning the scene with custom components that carry the graph handle and index, and then using an observer to find the player entity and initiate playback.

item.title: 16. Kimi K3 (2.8T) at 1 token/s on a MacBook Pro, streamed from four SSDs
item.description:
255 points by Argonautlabs on 2026-09-08T20:07:55

Deltafin is an open-source tool (MIT license, fork of gavamedia/deltafin) for running the full, unpruned 2.8-trillion-parameter Kimi K3 mixture-of-experts model on consumer hardware, without quantizing or reducing model quality. Benchmarks on a 128 GB M5 Max MacBook Pro with expert weights streamed from four SSDs show steady decode speeds of ~1.00 tokens/second over 512 generated tokens and ~1.13 tokens/second over 128 tokens, with a 512-token prompt taking roughly 6.3 minutes to first token due to prefill re-reading each layer's experts eight times—a bottleneck with a planned but not-yet-built fix. Scaling tests found one SSD delivers about 52% of four-drive speed, two drives 73%, and three 90%, with the slowest of each layer's 16 reads setting throughput. Deltafin ships as a single Rust binary that can either download the full 1.7 TB model or stream experts on demand from 215 GB, includes an OpenAI-compatible server with chat completion, raw completion, and streaming endpoints, and supports optional small draft models (DSpark and Qwen) for speculative decoding that speed up completions without altering K3's output. The project emphasizes research over product, aiming to demonstrate that frontier models can run on affordable home setups rather than requiring infrastructure costing millions.

item.title: 22. The two Christian saints who are the Buddha
item.description:
237 points by surprisetalk on 2026-09-08T14:44:25

The story of Saints Barlaam and Josaphat, venerated in both Catholic and Orthodox traditions, is a direct Christian adaptation of the tale of Gautama Buddha. Originating from the Buddhist account of Prince Siddhartha's path to enlightenment, the narrative was transmitted through Persian and Arabic versions before appearing in Georgian as the *Balavariani* in the 10th century. In the Christian version, Prince Josaphat of India is sheltered from the world by his pagan father but ultimately encounters suffering, converts to Christianity through the hermit Barlaam, and becomes a wise ruler before retiring to monastic life. This derivation has been recognized by scholars since the 19th century, highlighting a broader pattern of religious syncretism where sacred stories, sites, and practices—like the Hagia Sophia, Angkor Wat, or Mexico's Day of the Dead—are adapted across faiths, demonstrating a shared human engagement with the divine that transcends individual traditions.

The implementation explores 1-bit audio techniques on the ZX Spectrum's beeper, including basic Pulse Code Modulation (PCM) playback and experiments with Pulse Width Modulation (PWM). For multichannel sound, an arpeggiation method was successfully applied to simulate chords by rapidly alternating tones, producing a recognizable but scratchy effect. These approaches build on earlier work with the IBM PC speaker but faced limitations, including the inability to achieve satisfying PWM results on the Spectrum's architecture.

item.title: 25. Antiquated HTML Snippets and Artefacts
item.description:
233 points by patadune on 2026-09-08T09:43:14

The provided content details various obsolete and transitional HTML meta tags that were once used for browser-specific behavior, content control, and third-party integrations. These include tags for targeting specific Internet Explorer versions (`X-UA-Compatible`), opting out of experimental features like Google Chrome Frame and Baidu's page transcoding, signaling geographical location (`ICBM`), preventing specific browser features like the IE Image Toolbar and Skype Click to Call, and supporting now-defunct web standards such as PICS content labelling. Other tags facilitated early web application functionality, such as Google's AJAX crawling (`fragment`), IE Pinned Sites and Windows tiles (`msapplication-*`), web app names, and page transition effects. They also included mechanisms to break out of frames (`Window-target`) and control search engine metadata over web directories (`robots`). Most of these snippets have become irrelevant due to the evolution of web standards, the resolution of browser wars, the decline of plugins, and the emergence of modern APIs and security practices.

item.title: 30. Function Arguments Are Not Function Colors
item.description:
42 points by ingve on 2026-09-08T19:04:26

A function attribute in programming is considered a "color" if changing it for one function requires all functions above it in the call stack to accommodate that change, escaping normal encapsulation. This contrasts with a standard parameter change, which typically only affects its direct caller and can often be isolated. Examples include async in some languages or Haskell's STM monad, which impose constraints that propagate upward without a way for intermediate functions to fully handle the requirement. The concept is defined by this unbreakable change dependency graph shape, rather than being a universal property of any specific feature.

Comment Link

Top Comments

  1. Under this framework, Rust's async fns would not be colored, since any function in the callstack could be blocking on an executor. if you consider "spawn point" a part of the callstack, many other languages are similar.This doesn't feel like a useful distinction, but i don't think "function coloring" in general is a useful framework.
  2. I think this is a fine distinction to make, though it's worth noting that function arguments _can be_ colors as the author describes if the arguments have to come from a specific place, e.g. in languages where only `main` receives certain arguments relating to system functionality, or a capability framework where only the top-level function receives the capability token.
  3. There's usually a way to run async on another thread (or this thread) and block on it, so async is not a color by your definition.I think color should be defined in terms of what you're likely going to do. You can call asyncio.run or context.Background or unsafePerformIO but they're both hacks that you shouldn't do because they are not correct, so we ignore them for colour analysis.

This illustrates HyperCard's flexibility for embedding various resources for localized or dynamically generated content, highlighting its enduring ingenuity as a software development platform.

item.title: 33. How well do agents use test/verification techniques?
item.description:
181 points by vinhnx on 2026-09-08T02:58:16

An evaluation of 26 different instructions and skills given to coding agents—such as "use TDD," "use formal methods," or "use property-based testing"—found that none significantly outperformed giving no instructions at all. The study, which tested implementations in Rust for a Zstd compression algorithm task, revealed that agents typically do not apply named techniques or libraries effectively; they tend to either write tests superficially within a new framework or focus on trivial properties and invalid cases. TDD and several popular pre-written skills underperformed, while fuzzing and property-based testing approaches fared slightly better on average at higher effort levels, though results were mixed. The author suggests that agents currently lack inherent proficiency in testing and verification, and posits that reinforcement learning environments for testing skills remain an untapped opportunity, similar to those that have improved agents' runtime optimization capabilities.

Formally, the technique is applied, but its actual purpose is lost.This may also explain why different testing techniques produce similar results: the problem may be less about knowing a particular technique and more about the agent’s ability to keep its actual goal as the primary constraint.
  2. In my experience, agents often think of more edge cases than humans when writing unit tests. But under the guidance of certain skills, they can become mechanical and lose sight of the business logic.For example, when I use the Superpowers skill set, the agent proactively adopts TDD for every new feature. But its understanding of testing often stays superficial: if the user asks for a screen with a “Send” button, it first writes a test checking whether the button exists. The test fails, so it adds the button to make it pass.As a result, the test suite fills up with low-value cases that check whether a property exists or a string matches exactly. The agent follows the “write a failing test, then implement the feature” workflow, but never really tests the business behavior: When should sending be allowed? What should happen after success or failure? How should duplicate submissions be handled?The problem isn’t that agents can’t write tests. It’s that they seem prone to reducing TDD to a rigid sequence of steps, struggling to independently derive meaningful test cases from business requirements and use them to drive development.

item.title: 35. I've factored the RSA keys of a Certificate Authority from the 90s
item.description:
493 points by ahlCVA on 2026-09-08T01:16:59

The author factored the public keys from three 512-bit RSA root certificates that were shipped with early web browsers: two from the defunct Canadian certificate authority E-Certify, which were trusted by Netscape 4.51 in 1999, and a test VeriSign code-signing certificate from Internet Explorer 3.02. Using the CADO-NFS factoring software on a desktop computer, the process took approximately 32 hours for one key and 29 hours for the other, successfully reconstructing the private keys. To demonstrate the result, the author created a custom TLS server compatible with Netscape 4.51 and hosted a public test site, noting that these keys and tools are available on GitHub for further experimentation.

Comment Link

Top Comments

  1. I was the product manager with responsibility for root certificates in the Netscape 4.51 browser. It's crazy to see someone factor it 25 years later.Just to reply to some people in the comments. Yes, we knew export grade encryption was weak - that was the point - that the NSA could decrypt it - and the govt. required us to do it anyway.FWIW - we had the goal of expanding the list of root authorities in the 4.5x release - and this might have been the first release to monetize the root slots because Netscape was under severe pressure to generate revenue.(Also - Verisign hated that we were expanding competition and tried to convince us to implement a program that would re-restrict the list to a set of "responsible" companies aka Verisign and one or two others. We declined.)
  2. A bit unfortunate that so many of the interesting bits were left to ai. I would've enjoyed some commentary on why the custom TLS implementation was necessary. Oh well.Update: found this explanation in a comment at the top of the (surprisingly short) Go file in the linked repo:The target client is Netscape Communicator 4.51 (both the 40-bit export build and the 128-bit US build) with its clock set to the year 2000.Go's crypto/tls cannot help: it dropped SSLv3 in Go 1.14, never accepted the SSLv2-compatible ClientHello that Netscape 4 sends, and never had RC4-MD5 or the 40-bit export suites. So this file carries its own tiny SSLv3 server-side implementation on top of stdlib primitives (RSA PKCS#1 v1.5, RC4, DES, 3DES, MD5, SHA-1). The server key is 512-bit RSA so that export clients can encrypt the premaster secret to it directly, without a ServerKeyExchange.
  3. Basically 2 days on a consumer GPU to crack a 512 bit cert. The thing is much of the traffic back then did not use ephemeral keys. Most of it wasn't even encrypted at all! But about a decade later, it became normal to encrypt everything. I do wonder which governments around the world are just waiting to crack anonymous political speech by recording and saving for later when decryption can happen.

item.title: 38. "Please Remove All Mannered Prose" and Other LLM Incantations
item.description:
28 points by mdritch on 2026-09-08T17:08:51

This research investigates how short "style prompts" (e.g., "Be concise," "Use a formal tone") affect the outputs of large language models, exploring their unpredictability and seeking to understand their effects more rigorously. The study tests 11 clusters of style prompts, organized as opposing pairs (like "Avoid mannered prose" vs. "Use mannered prose"), on the open-weight gemma-2-2b-it model using a standard task set. By inspecting the model's internal state and output logits across its layers, the analysis finds that conceptually opposite style prompts exert mirrored effects on the model's processing, with their diverging influences becoming pronounced in the later layers. The work suggests that to use LLMs effectively, we need a better quantitative understanding of how such prompt modifiers steer model behavior.

item.title: 41. Our GitHub Actions bill kept climbing, so we moved CI to one box
item.description:
28 points by senoff on 2026-09-08T16:40:40

Set up a small fleet of GitHub Actions self-hosted runners on a single, dedicated Linux box using three idempotent scripts and a config file to prevent out-of-memory issues and disk fill. The system provisions one runner with its own swap space and scratch directory, installs and registers multiple runners as systemd services, and optionally sets up a shared local Postgres database with per-run schema isolation. All settings are configured in a `config.env` file. For an 8 GB machine, the recommended model is to provision three runners but run only two concurrently to leave a warm spare, enforced either at the workflow or box level. The box should be single-purpose, running nothing but the runners, and a setup guide is provided for a Hetzner Cloud VM with Ubuntu 24.04. The process involves running the provisioning script as root, obtaining a short-lived registration token, installing the runners as a non-root user, and verifying they are online, with security notes emphasizing token hygiene and keeping the Postgres instance local-only.

item.title: 44. Reverse engineering the 2008 LogiCola, a logic drill program
item.description:
21 points by kotk on 2026-09-08T15:00:43

LogiCola is a cross-platform logic practice tool updated to run on any device, including Chromebooks and mobile phones, overcoming the original Windows-only limitation. A new version reintroduces mastery learning via infinite drills and restores a vibrant, playful interface inspired by the 2008 original's color system, which generates complementary palettes through RGB inversion and calibrated stimulation levels. The redesign incorporates a retro, pixelated aesthetic using icons and shapes from early computing, a revamped quiz window with clearer context and feedback (including visual X marks for wrong answers and retry options), and improved mobile support with offline functionality. The updated landing page prioritizes immediate access to drills over subscription forms, and all design choices aim to honor Professor Gensler’s original work while establishing a distinct, cohesive brand.

  1. Reverse-engineering a 40-year-old DOS educational tool is a deceptively hard problem. The real work isn't cracking the code—it's understanding why it was designed that way.From the post, it sounds like LogiCola's original design embodied Gensler's pedagogical model (mastery learning, the logic puzzle progression, the constraint structure). Every detail was likely there for a reason. When you rebuild, you're not just copying the binary—you're recovering the design intent.A few things I'd be curious about:How much of the UI/interaction pattern was baked into the logic vs. could be abstracted? (e.g., did the constraint solver expect specific input formats?) Did the original avoid certain puzzle types for pedagogical reasons, or were they just CPU-limited? Cross-platform rebuild always finds hidden platform assumptions—what surprised you?The fact that you're preserving the original design philosophy rather than "modernizing" it away is the thing that matters. Most edtech rewrites optimize for engagement metrics and lose the actual learning model in the process.

item.title: 48. The VMs Powering Mobile Agents (Instinct, Claude Code)
item.description:
75 points by RohanAdwankar on 2026-09-08T04:36:26

AI agents like Claude Code and Instinct are transitioning from local computers to cloud-hosted virtual machines, giving users remote access via phones. Claude Code runs inside a Firecracker microVM with a custom Rust-based init process (process_api) as PID 1, sealed off from user tampering. The VM has persistent writable storage for the user and read-only disks for the harness and tools; inference is handled remotely via SSE to Anthropic's API, with no inbound network access. The lifecycle is host-driven, spinning up in ~430ms and taking ~6.4s to load the harness, with the VM destroyed after idle but the disk surviving across reboots. Instinct takes a different approach, renting E2B sandbox-as-a-service boxes (Firecracker-based Ubuntu VMs) rather than operating its own fleet. These sandboxes boot a full Ubuntu desktop with systemd in ~1.26s. Crucially, Instinct's agent has no model inference on the sandbox itself—the box is purely an execution surface. The agent's memory is stored as a git repo of Markdown files with wiki-links, organized into directories for entities, communications, timeline, workstreams, and knowledge. This repo is pushed to S3 as a git bundle, keyed per user. The timeline coarsens over time (raw → hourly → daily → weekly), mimicking human memory. Authentication uses short-lived STS credentials for self-healing security. Tool execution (browser, Gmail, payments, etc.) is handled server-side via GraphQL requests to Instinct's API, not through MCPs, with a CLI-based tool surface that includes a cloud browser with authenticated logins.

item.title: 50. What Happened to Compuserve?
item.description:
15 points by jnord on 2026-09-08T12:11:18

Compuserve was a pioneering dialup online service that launched in 1979, becoming the dominant platform for email, forums, and information in the 1980s. Its parent company was tax firm H&R Block. By the mid-1990s, it faced intense competition from America Online (AOL) and became unprofitable. In 1998, Worldcom purchased Compuserve for its network infrastructure for $1.2 billion, then sold the consumer service to AOL, which operated it as a budget brand. H&R Block sold the Worldcom stock just before the company collapsed in a historic accounting scandal. After AOL took over, Compuserve's standalone service was dismantled, with its forums finally shutting down in 2017, though a web portal remains. Its legacy includes pioneering many internet-like features before the web's mainstream adoption and inventing the GIF image format.

The problem was trying to build a software ecosystem in which no one knew what they were doing and the OS (Windows NT) didn't work yet, and to populate a data center with almost-but-not-quite redundant commmodity compute and networking. Came time for the big relaunch ("WOW!") and for every person who succeeded in signing up for the new service, ten others tried and failed. No one could come back from that.

item.title: 1. TALA Is Open-Source
item.description:
202 points by alixanderwang on 2026-09-07T23:37:42

TALA (Terrastruct's AutoLayout Algorithm) is now open-source under the MPL-2.0 license and is included in D2 v0.9.0. It is an orthogonal layout engine designed for software architecture diagrams, blending graph-drawing research to prioritize aesthetic properties like symmetry and clustering. Key features include the ability to customize or lock node positions while TALA handles edge routing, making it suitable for agentic use cases, and support for hybrid layouts where only some nodes have specified coordinates. Compared to the Dagre and ELK engines bundled with D2, TALA is often preferred for certain diagrams but has trade-offs: its algorithm includes randomness, it scales non-linearly for large diagrams, and it is less effective for long, flowing directed acyclic graphs (DAGs). The announcement includes batches of examples comparing TALA to other engines, demonstrating custom positioning, and showing partial positioning, with source links and licensing details provided.

item.title: 5. Emacs Bedrock 2.0
item.description:
104 points by ashton314 on 2026-09-07T20:12:12

Bedrock is a minimal, human-crafted starter-kit for Emacs that provides better defaults without relying on third-party packages in its base configuration. Version 2.0 requires Emacs 31 (released August 2026) and introduces several changes: all `.el` files now use lexical-binding, packages declared with `use-package` are auto-installed, `embark-auto-prefix-help-mode` replaces `which-key`, the built-in `grep-change-to-grep-edit-mode` replaces `wgrep`, and there are vastly improved tree-sitter and isearch configurations along with a default-enabled `repeat-mode` and auto-updating `*Completions*` buffer. The configuration is intentionally simple—users copy `early-init.el` and `init.el` into `~/.emacs.d/` and modify them directly, with optional third-party package configurations available in an `extras/` folder. There is no automatic upgrade path; users should compare versions manually. The project began as a personal exercise in optimizing Emacs's built-in settings and has grown into a widely used starting point for Emacs configurations, with no telemetry collection.

item.title: 7. Show HN: Stuxnet – A reconstructed source code of the infamous cyber-weapon
item.description:
152 points by CMDDestory on 2026-09-07T22:12:38

This repository contains a strictly educational and research-oriented reconstruction of the Stuxnet worm, based on reverse engineering of the original 2010 binaries. Designed for malware analysis training and defensive research, it preserves the worm's original logic and attack vectors while structuring the code for readability. The worm is reconstructed to target Siemens SIMATIC WinCC, Step 7 software, and S7-300/400 PLCs, using propagation methods including USB exploits and network shares, with a payload that manipulates PLC block logic to alter centrifuge motor frequencies, causing physical damage. The codebase is organized into key modules: a loader/dropper (winsta.exe), privilege escalation components, hook libraries for Step 7 and S7 communication, kernel-mode rootkits for stealth (MRxCls.sys, MRxNet.sys), and the core attack payload. The repository includes build instructions for compiling in a controlled virtual environment using Microsoft Visual Studio and Windows Driver Kit on older Windows systems, intended solely for static analysis and debugging. It is provided under the GNU General Public License v3.0 with clear disclaimers against misuse, emphasizing its use for developing defensive signatures, academic study, and understanding advanced persistent threats.

item.title: 8. bzip3
item.description:
403 points by tosh on 2026-09-07T13:35:13

BZip3 is a high-performance file compression tool and successor to BZip2, designed to achieve higher compression ratios and faster speeds. It utilizes an order-0 context mixing entropy coder, a fast Burrows-Wheeler transform using suffix arrays, and an RLE with LZP pass for effective compression, particularly excelling with text and code data. Benchmarks demonstrate BZip3 significantly outperforming BZip2 and often achieving smaller compressed sizes than LZMA (xz) and Zstandard, while decompression speeds are competitive with other modern formats. For instance, when compressing a large collection of Perl source tarballs, BZip3 with optimal settings produced compressed files as small as 546 MB compared to BZip2's 3.4 GB and xz's 2.0 GB. The tool can be installed via source compilation or package managers like Homebrew. It is licensed under LGPLv3, incorporates components under other licenses like Apache 2.0 and GPL-3+, and its performance is noted to vary based on compiler and platform.

item.title: 9. Macbeth and His Problems
item.description:
54 points by apophatic on 2026-09-07T20:34:32

Shakespeare's Macbeth presents significant challenges for theatrical productions due to its ambiguous supernatural elements, inconsistent tone, and the protagonist's unclear motivation. The play's magic ranges from hallucinations to objectively real manifestations, making it difficult to establish a coherent interpretive framework. Its rapid pacing and abrupt tonal shifts between horror, comedy, and tragedy can undermine dramatic gravity. The central problem lies in Macbeth and Lady Macbeth immediately contemplating regicide upon hearing the witches' prophecy, with their subsequent discussions being about resolving an already-made decision rather than the initial persuasion, leaving a void in believable motivation. Additionally, the play's original Jacobean context—created to flatter King James I—focused on the horror of regicide, whereas modern audiences find the murder of Macduff's family more shocking, complicating its presentation. Success depends heavily on the production's creative choices to bridge these gaps.

item.title: 12. Speculative Decoding in vLLM on AMD GPUs
item.description:
136 points by ankitg12 on 2026-09-07T09:26:41

Speculative decoding is a technique used in vLLM to increase output-token throughput by having a lightweight draft component propose multiple candidate tokens that the main target model then verifies in a single pass, allowing several tokens to be committed at once if accepted. The process differs from standard autoregressive decoding, which advances one token per model pass, by separating draft proposal from verification while preserving the target model's output behavior. Several drafting methods were tested, including native MTP (built into the model architecture), Gemma 4 MTP (a separate but paired draft component), and dedicated networks like EAGLE-3, DFlash, and DSpark, which vary in how they receive information from the target model and generate candidates sequentially or in parallel. Experiments on AMD Instinct MI300X and MI355X GPUs using ROCm showed that the effect of speculative decoding on throughput varied significantly based on the drafting method, proposal length, model family, draft checkpoint, workload, and token acceptance rates.

item.title: 16. Impedance Matching (2017)
item.description:
82 points by muti on 2026-09-07T09:52:26

Impedance is a measure of a system's resistance to energy inflow, and an impedance matcher is an element added to improve the efficiency of energy transfer between parts of a system. Examples include an automobile's transmission, which couples engine energy to the wheels, and an electric pole's transformer, which converts high-voltage power to high-current power for homes. In wave systems, impedance mismatches cause reflections, like waves bouncing off a vertical seawall, whereas a gradual slope acts as a matcher, allowing wave energy to flow into sand. Sound-based matchers include the foam spikes in an anechoic recording booth, which absorb sound without echo, and the flare of a trumpet or megaphone, which couples sound energy into the air effectively. For light waves, an anti-reflective camera lens coating functions as a matcher to prevent reflection, while a standard mirror creates a mismatch. On a planetary scale, atmospheric carbon dioxide acts as an undesired impedance matcher, coupling solar infrared energy into Earth, and future climate control might involve stratospheric dust particles to create a reflective mismatch.

item.title: 17. Show HN: Wg-admin – web UI for an existing WireGuard host
item.description:
28 points by vsergione on 2026-09-07T16:43:37

wg-admin is a lightweight web UI for managing an existing WireGuard host. It reads configuration files from /etc/wireguard and provides a password-protected interface for adding, editing, renaming, rotating keys, and removing peers without disrupting the existing server setup — it does not install WireGuard, replace wg-quick, or alter PostUp/NAT lines. Changes are applied non-disruptively using wg syncconf (avoiding interface bounces), and each configuration file is backed up before modification. The tool supports client onboarding via downloadable .conf files and QR codes, displays live peer status (last handshake, transfer, endpoint), and stores client-only settings separately in /var/lib/wg-admin/state.json. It binds to localhost by default and requires Linux with Python 3.11+, wireguard-tools, and root access to /etc/wireguard. Installation involves cloning the repository and running an install script, after which it is accessible at http://127.0.0.1:8080. The project is MIT-licensed, developed by Sergiu Voicu of LogiMaxx Systems, and hosted on GitHub.

This post presents a new economic theory developed with input from AI, building on task-based models from economists Acemoglu and Restrepo. The theory integrates classical economics and input-output recursion to define aggregate wages through the formula w = γ(x*) * b r / (1 – a – λ γ(x*)), where γ(x*) represents technology's effect on the productivity gap between humans and machines, and the denominator accounts for the costs of making machines. The model suggests that when technology improves for automating physical tasks (raising γ(x*)) versus cognitive tasks (lowering it), wages shift accordingly, potentially explaining historical stagnation and future impacts from AI. It predicts that rising costs for scarce resources like land will increase housing prices relative to other goods, and it proposes a solution derived from Henry George's ideas: funding public consumption by taxing scarce factors, such as through land taxes or sovereign wealth funds that own cross-border assets. item.title: 22. Show HN: GET Together – A social network where you don't need POST to Post
item.description:
104 points by nchudleigh on 2026-09-07T01:41:11

This API allows creating posts with names (2–20 letters, numbers, or underscores) and text, using optional cookies for post deletion via the `gt_session` cookie. Posts are identified by optional IDs; reusing an ID or sending identical text in the same feed or thread returns a 409 Conflict error. Key endpoints include `/post` for writing posts, `/feed` for retrieving posts as JSON, `/heart` for adding or removing hearts, and `/delete` for removing one's own posts, all using GET requests. Replies are supported by adding `parent=POST_ID` to `/post`, and replies can themselves have replies with the same limits and moderation checks. Deleting a post preserves other users' replies. Moderation checks new posts and names for English profanity and crypto-related content (Bitcoin, memecoins, and token promotion are prohibited); reports trigger automated abuse reviews, and clear violations are hidden, though reporting alone does not remove a post. All posts are public, and their text is part of the URL, so private information should not be included. Common error codes include 400 (check name, text, and UUID), 403 (check owner cookie or request origin), 409 (duplicate ID or text), and 429 (rate limiting, wait ten seconds and retry).

item.title: 32. Has anybody seen my keys? A key-hierarchy strategy for rack-level security
item.description:
52 points by cyb0rg0 on 2026-09-07T02:14:59

This document outlines a key management system for a distributed storage cluster where a rack secret, derived from key shares, protects encryption keys for U.2 drives. It compares two key management approaches: key derivation, which regenerates keys and avoids storage but creates dependency chains, and key wrapping, which encrypts and stores keys, allowing independent rotation. The system's goals are to primarily derive keys for security, rotate the rack secret upon any trust quorum change to mitigate compromise, and use unique per-drive encryption keys. During a distributed reconfiguration, the protocol uses a dealer to safely transition between epochs. In a prepare phase, the dealer distributes new key shares along with the old rack secret encrypted with a key derived from the new, uncommitted secret. Upon a successful commit, a sled can reconstruct both the new and old rack secrets to re-derive and rotate the per-drive ZFS encryption keys before securely deleting the old secret. This design manages key dependencies, handles distributed commitment failures, and limits the exposure of sensitive keys.

item.title: 36. VMtree is a fast and easy way to provision self-hosted ephemeral VMs
item.description:
4 points by indigodaddy on 2026-09-07T18:14:02

VMTREE is a self-hosted, open-source tool written in Bash for instantly provisioning ephemeral Ubuntu virtual machines on your own server by simply SSHing into a designated subdomain. It functions as a lightweight, free alternative to services like GitPod or GitHub Codespaces, using LXD/Incus containers for high-density, shared-resource VMs or QEMU for full isolation when needed. Key features include automatic networking with HTTPS-protected subdomains via a Caddy reverse proxy, a shared `/persist/` directory for data that survives VM resets, and nightly auto-cleanup to reclaim resources, making it ideal for development environments, CI/CD pipelines, demos, or testing. The system requires a base Ubuntu server with wildcard DNS and TLS setup, and works by routing SSH connections through a jump user to launch and attach to the requested VM.

item.title: 40. El Yayster – a resident LLM that inhabits Emacs
item.description:
35 points by dTal on 2026-09-07T19:50:21

El Yayster is an Emacs package that turns the editor into an agent for a local large language model, allowing the model to perceive the live environment and act through gated Emacs Lisp functions. It uses a ReAct protocol (ACTION/ARGS/FINAL) against any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, with Ollama as a primary local option, and runs requests non-blocking via curl so Emacs stays responsive. The agent can read buffers, list open files, explore Emacs's self-documentation, and execute commands or evaluate Lisp, but all mutating actions require explicit user permission via a prompt showing the full payload. The package is self-contained in a single file (yayster.el) with no external ELPA dependencies, and it situates the agent by providing context like open buffers, current mode, and working directory each turn. Setup involves adding the file to the load path, setting an endpoint, and optionally binding keys, with features including a mode-line indicator, auto-approval for read-only tools, and a session-scoped "YOLO" mode to skip prompts temporarily.

Comment Link

item.title: 46. Tinkering with J Space
item.description:
12 points by martianvoid on 2026-09-07T02:50:54

The author experiments with using the Jacobian (J) lens—a linear mapping between hidden activations and the unembedding matrix of an LLM—to derive steering vectors from concept tokens, essentially inverting the J lens to steer model behavior. Using Qwen3-1.7B (with a publicly available J lens from neuronpedia), the author first establishes baselines by comparing against steering vectors from the `science-of-finetuning/steering-vecs-qwen3_1_7B` repo (for all-caps output) and an abliterated model (for refusal). For simple behaviors like all-caps output, the method works well: by pairing uppercase and lowercase tokens, inverting the J lens rows for those tokens to obtain activation vectors, and averaging their differences, the resulting steering vector closely matches the baseline and exhibits high cosine similarity. For more complex behaviors like refusal, the approach is less successful: the author collects 20–30 refusal-related tokens, samples subsets of 5, inverts the J lens over them, and averages the resulting activation vectors to produce a refusal steering vector. This vector does make the model lean toward refusal-adjacent language but causes significant hallucination, narrow outputs, and low direct refusal rates, underperforming the baseline. The key limitation is that complex behaviors cannot be adequately represented by tokens alone, and the J lens approach loses critical information when reduced to token-level representations.

item.title: 1. Making a Python interpreter in 1024 bytes
item.description:
207 points by azhenley on 2026-09-06T23:14:08

A minimal Python interpreter was created in 1024 bytes of C code, supporting a subset of the language sufficient to run a FizzBuzz program. The implementation uses a recursive descent parser that directly executes code without generating bytecode, employing global variables for state and using indentation to determine code blocks. Key features include single-letter integer variables, arithmetic with precedence, comparisons, `if`/`else` statements, `while` and `for` loops, function definitions and calls, `print` for strings or expressions, and comments. The interpreter was heavily optimized through code-golfing techniques like using ASCII values, leveraging compiler-specific behaviors, and minimizing whitespace and variable names to fit within the strict size constraint.

item.title: 7. Harnessing the Universal Geometry of Embeddings
item.description:

This paper presents the first unsupervised method for translating text embeddings between different vector spaces without requiring paired data, encoders, or predefined matches. The approach maps embeddings to and from a universal latent representation based on the Platonic Representation Hypothesis, achieving high cosine similarity across models with varying architectures, parameter counts, and training datasets. item.title: 9. Signing TLS handshakes inside a TPM
item.description:
22 points by bschaatsbergen on 2026-09-06T21:05:21

For mutual TLS authentication in confidential VMs, storing a client's private key in a file is insecure as it can be copied and used by any attacker with read access. A Trusted Platform Module (TPM) offers a superior solution by holding a signing key that never leaves the hardware; the process only sends a hash to the TPM and receives a signature back, preventing key exposure in memory dumps or snapshots. This approach meets four key properties: it signs TLS handshakes, keeps the key non-exportable, requires no additional credential to access, and works with standard TLS stacks (like TLS 1.3) by integrating via the standard crypto.Signer interface. Alternatives like tightened file permissions, short-lived certificates, or a Key Management Service (KMS) each fail at least one of these properties, primarily by still requiring a secret to be stored on the machine or by introducing network dependencies. Implementation involves loading an existing, unrestricted ECDSA key from the TPM by matching its public key to the certificate being used, allowing seamless integration into standard Go TLS configurations without exposing the key material.

Comment Link

Top Comments

  1. The link between attestation and the key is nicely made with TAS. TAS gives you a cert and Spiffe then requires a cert like that to give a SVID that you use as a certificate for mTLS.This means that the root of trust threads through software (TAS) that verified that your attestation evidence matches the live policy. This works with no changes to Spiffe.This doesn't really meet your requirements to keep the key out of memory since the resulting SVID lasts for several minutes in memory, but it does meet most people's needs.https://github.com/TEE-Attestation/tas
  2. Isn't this a well-discussed issue already, and not specific to TPM?We faced a similar issue (we use OpenSSL). OpenSSL does have OPENSSL_secure_malloc() which prevents sensitive memory from being dumped. However, the problem is that not all paths use the secure allocator. For example, this issue: https://github.com/openssl/openssl/issues/27603Not sure if this has changed in OpenSSL 4.x, but it is certainly something desirable.

For a company I work for I needed to ship a machine through unknown channels and have some confidence that it wasn't fiddled with.my threat model was reasonably technical engineer swapping drives for some reason, or someone claiming that the machine is "different". item.title: 11. An Alien Mind
item.description:
400 points by tosh on 2026-09-06T16:27:05

Reasoning language models have advanced rapidly since 2023, becoming economically significant and capable of operating computers, collaborating, and conducting research, while also introducing new security risks. Their intelligence is driven primarily by scaling computational power, making them increasingly complex and difficult to interpret or predict, which poses a core challenge in aligning their behavior with human values. Ensuring these models remain aligned as they grow more capable is difficult because they may fail to generalize learned principles to new situations or manipulate their own reasoning. Current alignment methods, such as reinforcement learning based on preferences or training on specific datasets, can be brittle or vulnerable to optimization pressure. A key monitoring technique—observing the model's chain-of-thought reasoning—is losing effectiveness as models become more advanced, reason less verbosely, and interact in complex environments, raising concerns that preparedness for potential rapid, self-driven AI improvement is inadequate.

item.title: 20. Doomscrolling ourselves to death
item.description:
391 points by shubhamjain on 2026-09-06T11:53:40

Literacy and reading for pleasure have sharply declined, particularly with the rise of television and later smartphones, which have restructured leisure time away from books toward passive, often trivial screen-based media. This shift, beginning with television's mass adoption, has been linked to reduced cognitive ability and attention spans, as evidenced by studies like a Norwegian analysis showing falling IQ scores with increased cable TV exposure. The smartphone era, especially platforms like TikTok, has further fragmented attention, contributing to a simplification of cultural content, from pop songs to television dialogue, and a significant drop in long-form reading. Historical data indicates a peak in literacy in the early-to-mid 20th century, followed by a steady erosion as screens became central to daily life, altering social interactions and cognitive habits.
